content: The systematic reviews and recommendations were based on a prioritization process conducted by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Following an initial meeting, GDG members completed a survey to rank clinical questions and outcomes by their relevance and importance. Nine PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions were identified to guide updates on the treatment of early and late syphilis, as well as congenital syphilis. Only outcomes deemed critical or important to patients and decision-making were included, such as serological response, clinical cure, transmission to partners, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), compliance, HIV transmission or acquisition, sexually transmitted infection (STI) complications, and adverse effects (including maternal and fetal outcomes in pregnant women). The systematic reviews for each priority question were conducted by McMaster University, a WHO Collaborating Centre for Evidence-Informed Policy. Evidence was gathered from both published and unpublished literature, focusing on desirable and undesirable outcomes, patient values and preferences, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility. Comprehensive searches for systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and non-randomized studies were performed up to April 2015. Two members of the review team screened studies, extracted and analyzed data, and assessed the quality of evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. The guidelines were developed following the 2014 WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The quality of evidence was categorized into four levels: high (very confident in the effect estimate), moderate (moderately confident, with some possibility of substantial differences), low (limited confidence, with potential for substantial differences), and very low (very little confidence, with likely substantial differences). Direct costs of medicines were estimated using the 2014 MSH International Drug Price Indicator Guide. All evidence was summarized in GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision frameworks. Recommendations were formulated during a second GDG meeting in October 2015, facilitated by co-chairs with expertise in GRADE methodology and clinical STI management. The GDG considered the benefits and harms of interventions, the value placed on outcomes, costs, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility. Consensus was reached for all recommendations without the need for voting. Final recommendations were approved electronically by all GDG members and subsequently peer-reviewed. Recommendations were rated as either strong (using The WHO STI guideline recommends...) or conditional (using The WHO STI guideline suggests...), with implications for patients, clinicians, and policymakers clearly outlined. Conflict of interest management was a priority throughout the guideline development process. Declarations of Interest (DOI) were obtained from all GDG members, and no significant financial or commercial conflicts related to STI treatment were identified. Minor interests, such as non-commercial grants, were deemed not to affect participation. The guidelines will be disseminated as a printed publication, a downloadable resource on the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research website, and through the WHO Reproductive Health Library. They will also be available in a guideline application created with GRADEpro GDT software. WHO will collaborate with regional and national partners to support the adaptation, implementation, and monitoring of these guidelines in sexual and reproductive health programs. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating recommendations will be established within a year of implementation, and user feedback will be collected via electronic surveys to identify challenges, evaluate usefulness, and address gaps in future editions. The guidelines emphasize the importance of adapting recommendations to local epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance patterns. In the absence of local data, the guidelines can be adopted as presented. Medicines recommended for STI treatment should meet criteria such as high efficacy (≥95% cure rate), low cost, low toxicity, and suitability for oral or single-dose administration. Benzathine penicillin G remains the preferred treatment for syphilis due to its historical success, ability to cross the placental barrier (critical for preventing mother-to-child transmission), and low risk of resistance. Alternative treatments, such as doxycycline or azithromycin, are suggested only in specific circumstances, with caution due to potential resistance and limitations in treating pregnant women. For congenital syphilis, infants with confirmed or suspected infection require prompt treatment. Benzathine penicillin G is recommended as the first-line therapy, with erythromycin or ceftriaxone suggested only when penicillin is unavailable. The GDG highlighted the importance of avoiding stock-outs of benzathine penicillin, particularly in antenatal care, to prevent severe complications in fetuses and newborns.
